q: What is the Manage Project Knowledge process?
options: Recording the project's status for the steering committee
Using existing knowledge and creating new knowledge for the objectives
Writing the procedures the team must follow on every single task
Storing every single project document in the document management system
explanation: Manage Project Knowledge is the process of using existing knowledge and creating new knowledge to achieve the project's objectives and contribute to organizational learning.

q: Which of these is a key benefit of the Manage Project Knowledge process?
options: It produces the cost baseline for the project
It identifies every stakeholder of the project
It ensures the product meets its quality metrics
It collects new knowledge for future projects
explanation: Its key benefits are using prior organizational knowledge to produce or improve the outcome, and collecting new knowledge created by the project to support operations and future projects or phases.

q: A team keeps its build procedures and configuration settings in a shared wiki. What kind of knowledge is this?
options: Explicit knowledge
Tacit knowledge
Emotional intelligence
Political awareness
explanation: Explicit knowledge is formal and systematic and can be codified in words, pictures or numbers, such as manuals, procedures and documented processes. It is easily shared through information management tools.

q: A senior engineer can tell from a machine's sound that a bearing will soon fail, but cannot explain how. What kind of knowledge is this?
options: Explicit knowledge
Codified knowledge
Tacit knowledge
Historical information
explanation: Tacit knowledge is personal and embedded in a person's mind: technical skills, experience, insights and practical knowledge. It is difficult to articulate and challenging to transfer.

q: Why is documenting explicit knowledge not enough on its own, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: Because documents can never be shared outside the team
Because codified knowledge lacks context and can be misread
Because explicit knowledge costs more than tacit knowledge
Because the lessons learned register is read only at closure
explanation: Codified explicit knowledge lacks context and is open to different interpretations, so although it is easier to share, it is not always understood or applied the right way.

q: What does the PMBOK Guide name as an important objective of knowledge management?
options: Replacing all meetings with written documentation
Keeping knowledge within the team that created it
Recording lessons only once the project has closed
Turning tacit knowledge into explicit where possible
explanation: An important objective of knowledge management is converting tacit knowledge into explicit knowledge when possible.

q: A key engineer leaves in a month and is the only person who understands a critical interface. What should the project manager do?
options: Start transferring the knowledge now through pairing and shadowing
Ask the engineer to write everything down on the very last working day
Ask the functional manager to postpone the engineer's departure
Let the replacement learn the interface on their own once hired
explanation: Identifying knowledge critical to the project and transferring it early is the point of the task. Tacit knowledge moves through interaction, such as work shadowing, so it cannot be captured in a last-day document alone.

q: How do generalizing specialists help keep knowledge from becoming a bottleneck on an agile team?
options: They own all of the documentation, so others never need to read it
They are the only people allowed to change critical code
Their breadth lets them help one another and avoid bottlenecks
They work alone on specialist tasks to avoid interruptions
explanation: Generalizing specialists have T-shaped skills, one specialty plus breadth, which lets them help one another and avoid bottlenecks. People with only one deep skill are I-shaped.

q: According to the PMBOK Guide, what determines which knowledge management tools suit a project?
options: The contract type and the number of vendors involved
Innovation, complexity and the diversity of the team
The size of the budget and the length of the schedule
The sponsor's personal preference for certain tools
explanation: The appropriate tools and techniques depend on the nature of the project, especially the degree of innovation, project complexity, and the level of diversity, including diversity of disciplines, among team members.

q: When is the lessons learned register created?
options: At project closure, when the final report is written
After the first major problem occurs on the project
Only when the sponsor asks for lessons to be kept
Early on, as an output of Manage Project Knowledge
explanation: The lessons learned register is created as an output of Manage Project Knowledge early in the project, then used as an input and updated as an output in many processes throughout.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Lessons learned register

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Lessons learned register

q: Which content does the PMBOK Guide say a lessons learned register may include?
options: Impacts, recommendations and proposed actions
Salaries and ratings of each team member
The signed contract and payments to suppliers
Each stakeholder's contact details and power
explanation: The register may include the category and description of the situation, its impacts, recommendations and proposed actions: challenges, problems, realized risks and opportunities.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Lessons learned register

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Lessons learned register

q: Who captures lessons learned, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: Only the project management office, after closure
Only the project manager, in the final project report
The persons or teams who were involved in the work
An external auditor appointed by the sponsor
explanation: The persons or teams involved in the work are also involved in capturing the lessons learned, by any suitable means, including video, pictures or audio.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Lessons learned register

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Lessons learned register

q: After a major milestone, the team holds a structured review of what happened, why it happened, and how to do better. What is this technique?
options: Benchmarking
After-action review
Stakeholder analysis
Earned value analysis
explanation: After-action reviews are a simple, structured process to analyze what happened, why, and how it can be done better. They are typically held at the end of a project or after significant milestones.

q: How does an in-progress postmortem differ from a traditional postmortem?
options: It is held only by people from outside the team
It replaces the lessons learned register entirely
It looks only at financial performance and costs
It is held at various stages, not only at the end
explanation: An in-progress postmortem is conducted at various stages of the life cycle to analyze performance, identify issues and implement improvements, unlike traditional postmortems held at the end of a project.

q: How does the PMBOK Guide describe retrospectives in relation to lessons learned?
options: As a form of lessons learned meeting, held frequently
As a replacement for every other form of lessons learned
As a meeting held only once, at the end of the project
As a status meeting for reporting to the sponsor
explanation: Retrospectives are a form of lessons learned meeting conducted frequently, at minimum at the end of each iteration. The term is used mostly in adaptive approaches but can refer to any lessons learned session.

q: Information management tools are most effective for sharing which kind of knowledge?
options: Deep tacit expertise that is hard to explain
Personal insights shared through conversation
Simple, unambiguous, codified explicit knowledge
The emotional reactions of the team to change
explanation: Information management tools create and connect people to information; they are effective for sharing simple, unambiguous, codified explicit knowledge.

q: How can information management tools be made more effective, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: By restricting access to the project manager only
By adding interaction, such as contacting a lesson's author
By printing every lesson and keeping it in a library
By deleting any lesson that is more than a year old
explanation: Tools that connect people to information can be enhanced by adding interaction, for example a "contact me" function so users can ask the originators of lessons for advice specific to their project.

q: A team uses an AI tool to summarize interviews and capture project knowledge. Which risks does the PMBOK Guide highlight?
options: Higher licensing costs and slower meetings
Fewer retrospectives and longer iterations
Lower team morale and more frequent conflicts
Exposing sensitive information and hallucinations
explanation: AI can be a significant source of knowledge, but significant risks include unintentionally exposing sensitive information and AI hallucinations. Projects should have responsible AI policies.

q: According to the Sixth Edition of the PMBOK Guide, what is the most important part of knowledge management?
options: An atmosphere of trust so people want to share
Choosing the best knowledge management software
Writing detailed procedures for every activity
Holding one lessons learned meeting at closure
explanation: Because knowledge resides in people's minds and people cannot be forced to share it, the most important part of knowledge management is creating an atmosphere of trust so that people are motivated to share.

q: Team members on a hybrid project rarely share what they know, although a new document system was introduced. What should the project manager focus on?
options: Making entries in the document system mandatory for all
Replacing the system with a more advanced platform
Building trust and giving people chances to share
Asking the sponsor to link bonuses to documents written
explanation: Even the best knowledge management tools will not work if people are not motivated to share. Tacit knowledge is shared by fostering a collaborative, trust-filled environment with opportunities for interaction.

q: Specialists from several projects meet regularly to share experience in their field. Which knowledge management tool is this?
options: A lessons learned register
A community of practice
A responsibility matrix
A work breakdown structure
explanation: Communities of practice, sometimes called communities of interest, and special interest groups are knowledge management tools that connect people to share and create knowledge.

q: A new tester spends two weeks alongside an experienced tester to learn how she handles difficult test cases. Which technique is this?
options: Benchmarking
Information gathering
Document analysis
Work shadowing
explanation: Work shadowing and reverse shadowing are knowledge management tools that let people learn tacit knowledge by working alongside someone.

q: Which technique does the PMBOK Guide describe as particularly effective for transferring tacit knowledge?
options: Storytelling
Document analysis
Library services
Web searches
explanation: Stories are particularly effective for transferring tacit knowledge, which is often difficult to articulate through formal documentation, by making lessons relatable and memorable.

q: On an agile team, how does pairing or mobbing with rotating roles help knowledge transfer?
options: It lets one expert do all critical work without interruption
It replaces the need for retrospectives and product reviews
Everyone drives and reviews work, exposing gaps early
It reduces the number of people who know the code base
explanation: Pairing or mobbing with rotating roles involves every person in both driving and reviewing work. This uncovers knowledge gaps early and builds collective ownership of quality.

q: What does the PMBOK Guide say AI tools such as interview bots add to managing project knowledge?
options: A full replacement for mentoring and conversation
Strong capabilities for capturing tacit and explicit knowledge
A guarantee that the captured knowledge is always correct
A way to manage knowledge without responsible AI policies
explanation: The latest AI technologies, such as interview bots, add strong capabilities in capturing and sharing both tacit and explicit knowledge, alongside risks that call for responsible AI policies.

q: Which THREE are tools and techniques of the Manage Project Knowledge process?
options: Storytelling
After-action reviews
Information management
Earned value analysis
Critical path method
Make-or-buy analysis
explanation: Figure 2-8 lists expert judgment, knowledge management, information management, after-action reviews, in-progress postmortems, storytelling, retrospective meetings, and interpersonal and team skills.

q: Which TWO are knowledge management tools that connect people, rather than information management tools?
options: Communities of practice
Knowledge fairs and cafés
Library services
Web searches
Document management systems
explanation: Knowledge management tools connect people: networking, communities of practice, shadowing, forums, events, workshops, knowledge fairs and cafés, interactive training. Libraries, web searches and the PMIS are information management tools.

q: Which TWO are characteristics of tacit knowledge in the PMBOK Guide?
options: Difficult to articulate
Experience-based
Easily codified in words
Formal and systematic
Shared mainly through manuals
explanation: Tacit knowledge is personal and embedded, difficult to articulate, experience-based and challenging to transfer. Being codifiable, formal and systematic, and shared through manuals are marks of explicit knowledge.

q: Match each way of capturing lessons with when it is used.
right: At least at the end of each iteration
At the end of a project or after major milestones
At various stages, to improve as the project goes
Created early and updated throughout the project
explanation: Retrospectives happen at least every iteration; after-action reviews typically at the end or after significant milestones; in-progress postmortems at various stages; the lessons learned register is created early and updated throughout.

q: Complete each statement about project knowledge.

Tacit knowledge is shared mainly through

explanation: Explicit knowledge, such as manuals and procedures, is codified and easily shared through documents. Tacit knowledge resides in people's minds and is often shared through conversations and interactions between people.
